question: A 48-year-old male presents with hoarseness for 8 weeks. He smokes 20 cigarettes/day for 25 years and drinks alcohol regularly. Which statement best describes his risk and the correct clinical action?

answers.text: His hoarseness is most likely due to vocal cord nodules from smoking; reassure and advise voice rest

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Vocal cord nodules are common in smokers, but hoarseness lasting more than 3 weeks in a smoker is a red flag for laryngeal carcinoma. Reassurance without laryngoscopy at 8 weeks is a dangerous management error. Tobacco and alcohol are synergistic co-carcinogens for HNSCC — this patient's pack-year history puts him at significantly elevated risk.

answers.text: Hoarseness persisting for more than 3 weeks in a heavy smoker is a red flag requiring urgent laryngoscopy to exclude laryngeal carcinoma

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The 3-week rule for hoarseness is a clinical standard: any hoarseness lasting more than 3 weeks in a patient over 45 with smoking history requires laryngoscopy to exclude glottic carcinoma. Tobacco and alcohol are synergistic (risk multiplies, not merely adds). Glottic carcinoma presents early with hoarseness, which is why it has the best prognosis of all laryngeal cancers — early detection is achievable and this opportunity must not be missed.

answers.text: Alcohol is not a risk factor for laryngeal cancer; only tobacco causes laryngeal malignancy

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Alcohol IS an independent risk factor for HNSCC, and when combined with tobacco, the risk is synergistic (multiplicative rather than additive). This is a high-yield fact for ENT cancer screening. Alcohol acts as a solvent that potentiates mucosal carcinogen absorption.

answers.text: Supraglottic carcinoma is more common than glottic carcinoma and presents earlier because of hoarseness

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This is the reverse of the correct fact. Glottic carcinoma presents EARLIER with hoarseness (because even a small lesion on the true vocal cord affects voice) and has the best prognosis. Supraglottic carcinoma is clinically silent until advanced, presenting late with referred otalgia, dysphagia, or neck nodes — making its prognosis worse.

overallFeedback.feedback: Hoarseness >3 weeks + smoker >45 years = red flag = laryngoscopy urgently. Tobacco and alcohol are synergistic. Glottic carcinoma presents early with hoarseness; supraglottic is late and silent until advanced.
Correct. The 3-week hoarseness rule in a smoker = urgent laryngoscopy. This is one of the most important early detection opportunities in ENT oncology.
